belief: My loved one who died by suicide can never be with God.
meta: A Christian look at the belief that a loved one who died by suicide can never be with God, with Scripture, questions, and homework for finding hope in the truth.
origins: Teaching that suicide is an unforgivable sin. Fear that because there was no chance to repent, salvation was lost. Painful comments from others after the loss. Deep grief mixed with confusion, anger, and guilt. Not knowing what Scripture actually says.
teaches: Suicide is a deep tragedy, and grief after it is especially heavy. But Scripture does not name it as an unforgivable sin. A believer’s salvation rests on Christ’s finished work, not on a final act or final confession. Nothing in all creation can separate those in Christ from the love of God. Many who die by suicide are suffering from illness and overwhelming pain. We cannot see a person’s heart, but we can trust the Judge of all the earth, who is just and full of mercy.
self_statements: They can’t be in heaven because of how they died.
Suicide is the one sin God won’t forgive.
They didn’t have time to repent, so they’re lost.
God rejected them in their worst moment.
errors: Treating one act as the whole story of a person’s relationship with God.
Assuming you know your loved one’s final standing with God.
Blaming yourself for another person’s choice in unbearable pain.
Believing suicide is unforgivable without biblical basis.
questions: Does Scripture call suicide an unforgivable sin?
Does salvation rest on a final confession or on Christ’s work?
What does Romans 8:38–39 say can separate believers from God’s love?
Could illness and pain have played a part in what happened?
Do I know everything that was in my loved one’s heart?
Can I trust the Judge of all the earth to be just and merciful?
Am I carrying blame that is not mine to carry?
truth: Suicide is a tragedy, but Scripture does not teach that it is unforgivable. Salvation rests on Christ’s finished work, and nothing in all creation can separate those in Christ from God’s love. I cannot see my loved one’s heart, but I can trust a just and merciful God with them. I do not have to carry blame for their choice.
